content.content:
<!--
SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
-->

# M9 plan: packaging a release

A plan for the owner to review, written by the spec side (session
evening-1024) before M9 starts. Nothing here is built. It takes its facts
from HARDWARE-SPEC.md (HW-n), from FM-1-RE's boot, architecture and update
documents (cited as RE, at the commit HARDWARE-SPEC.md's sources table
names), from the JieLi AC79 SDK (cited as SDK, at its pinned commit), and
from FM1 Open's terms files and file list only (docs/PLAN.md, Risks). It
quotes no code from any of them. The owner answered its questions on
2026-10-25 (recorded by session owner-answers-1025, at the end): M9 is
the app release only (section 1); section 2 stays a plan for M10.

M9 has two deliverables (docs/PLAN.md, "M1 to M9"): a release the
F-Emulator app can run, and the groundwork for a package real hardware can
install. Level 2 (M10 to M12) does the hardware itself; M9 does not flash
a unit.

## 1. A release for the app

The app boots a raw image (docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md, patch 0006): the same
flat binary fwtest runs, linked to start at `0x02000000` (HW-1). The build
already makes it reproducibly (R-REPRO-3) as `app.bin`, with `app.elf`
and a `SHA256SUMS` beside it.

A release is a folder (and a `.zip` of it) attached to a signed git tag
(`m9`, `v0.x.y`; app releases start at 0.9.0, answer 6):

| File | What |
|------|------|
| `small-beeps-<version>.bin` | the raw image, byte for byte the build's `app.bin` |
| `small-beeps-<version>.elf` | the same build's ELF, for symbols (optional for users) |
| `release.json` | metadata, below |
| `SHA256SUMS` | SHA-256 of every file above, in `sha256sum` format |
| `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` | this repository's licence and notices, as at the tag |
| `RELEASE-NOTES.md` | what changed, the test record's CI run, known limits |

`release.json`, one object:

- `name`, `version` (semantic), `git_commit` (full SHA), `tag`;
- `image`: file name, size, SHA-256, `load_address` `0x02000000`,
  `entry` `0x02000000` (HW-1, HW-2), `ram_used` (data + bss + stacks,
  from the build's size report);
- `toolchain`: the pinned toolchain's SHA-256 (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md) and the
  build container's image digest (R-REPRO-2);
- `fwtest`: the pinned image digest the release's suite ran on, and the
  CI run that recorded it;
- `store`: the store's chip region and format version
  (docs/STORE-FORMAT.md), so a user knows whether saved patches carry
  over between releases;
- `targets`: `["f-emulator-app"]` for this release kind.

What the firmware side needs: nothing new in the firmware. A
`tools/release.sh` that runs `tools/build.sh build`, checks the outputs
against the commit's CI record (`tools/reproduce`, R-REPRO-4), writes
`release.json` and `SHA256SUMS`, and stops if the tree is dirty or the tag
is missing. A CI job that rebuilds the tag and compares the hashes. A new
requirement (R-REL-1, say): a release's image is byte-identical to the
reproducible build of its tag, and its metadata and checksums match it.

How the app takes it: the app reads `release.json`, shows the release's
version, and checks the image's SHA-256 against it (answer 1). That is
the app's change, not the firmware's; the owner makes it in the app.

## 3. Risks

- **Bricking a unit.** A package the loader rejects after step 2 has begun
  writing can leave no runnable app. FM-1-RE records a recovery through
  the stock updater only while an app still runs; a hard brick needs
  JieLi's USB recovery, which M10 must prove on a unit first. No package
  goes near a unit before M10's recovery kit works.
- **The stock updater may refuse our package.** Its step-1 check is not
  fully understood (RE); a package with a new app and the stock loaders
  is the case most likely to pass, untested.
- **The key and encryption.** The app area is encrypted with the chip's
  key; if the packaging tool can't do that for us (or the key is per
  unit), the loader won't run our image. RE says the key in the loader's
  configuration is `0x980F` for the stock package; whether it is the same
  on every unit is not stated.
- **Licences.** FM1 Open's grant names "M-VAVE FM1 devices" only for its
  binary engine library, not for the boot files (docs/PLAN.md); still,
  check the grant's exact wording when vendoring. JieLi's Windows tools
  have no licence of their own (as with the toolchain): we would run
  them, never redistribute them.
- **Store survival across updates (Q-24).** If an update rewrites the VM
  or USR regions, or more, saved patches might be lost; ours sit in
  `0xFC000`-`0xFEFFF`, which the stock layout leaves unused.
- **Clean-room boundaries.** The stock `.fwsc` is stock firmware: no
  session opens it, and FM1 Open's copy is never vendored. FM-1-RE's
  update documents are allowed (CONTRIBUTING.md); its `firmware-images/`,
  disassembly and its OTA tool's code are not, and nor is its storage
  document for the firmware side (since evening-1024).
- **The app's loader is not the chip's loader.** A release that runs in
  the app (section 1) proves nothing about the chip's boot (HW-81, Q-11,
  Q-22). The two kinds of release are kept apart in their names and
  metadata.

## 4. The owner's answers (2026-10-25)

The questions were:

1. **The app and `release.json`.** Should the F-Emulator app read the
   metadata (show the version; check the hash), or keep loading a bare
   `.bin`?
2. **Release scope for M9.** Only the app release (section 1) in M9, with
   the hardware package left as this plan until M10's recovery kit
   exists? (Recommended.)

# M9 plan: packaging a release

A plan for the owner to review, written by the spec side (session
evening-1024) before M9 starts. Nothing here is built. It takes its facts
from HARDWARE-SPEC.md (HW-n), from FM-1-RE's boot, architecture and update

names), from the JieLi AC79 SDK (cited as SDK, at its pinned commit), and
from FM1 Open's terms files and file list only (docs/PLAN.md, Risks). It
quotes no code from any of them. The owner answered its questions on
2026-10-25 (recorded by session owner-answers-1025, at the end): M9 is
the app release only (section 1); section 2 stays a plan for M10.

M9 has two deliverables (docs/PLAN.md, "M1 to M9"): a release the
F-Emulator app can run, and the groundwork for a package real hardware can
install. Level 2 (M10 to M12) does the hardware itself; M9 does not flash
a unit.

## 1. A release for the app

The app boots a raw image (docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md, patch 0006): the same
flat binary fwtest runs, linked to start at `0x02000000` (HW-1). The build
already makes it reproducibly (R-REPRO-3) as `app.bin`, with `app.elf`
and a `SHA256SUMS` beside it.

A release is a folder (and a `.zip` of it) attached to a signed git tag
(`m9`, `v0.x.y`; app releases start at 0.9.0, answer 6):

| File | What |
|------|------|
| `small-beeps-<version>.bin` | the raw image, byte for byte the build's `app.bin` |
| `small-beeps-<version>.elf` | the same build's ELF, for symbols (optional for users) |
| `release.json` | metadata, below |
| `SHA256SUMS` | SHA-256 of every file above, in `sha256sum` format |
| `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` | this repository's licence and notices, as at the tag |
| `RELEASE-NOTES.md` | what changed, the test record's CI run, known limits |

`release.json`, one object:

- `name`, `version` (semantic), `git_commit` (full SHA), `tag`;
- `image`: file name, size, SHA-256, `load_address` `0x02000000`,
  `entry` `0x02000000` (HW-1, HW-2), `ram_used` (data + bss + stacks,
  from the build's size report);
- `toolchain`: the pinned toolchain's SHA-256 (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md) and the
  build container's image digest (R-REPRO-2);
- `fwtest`: the pinned image digest the release's suite ran on, and the
  CI run that recorded it;
- `store`: the store's chip region and format version
  (docs/STORE-FORMAT.md), so a user knows whether saved patches carry
  over between releases;
- `targets`: `["f-emulator-app"]` for this release kind.

What the firmware side needs: nothing new in the firmware. A
`tools/release.sh` that runs `tools/build.sh build`, checks the outputs
against the commit's CI record (`tools/reproduce`, R-REPRO-4), writes
`release.json` and `SHA256SUMS`, and stops if the tree is dirty or the tag
is missing. A CI job that rebuilds the tag and compares the hashes. A new
requirement (R-REL-1, say): a release's image is byte-identical to the
reproducible build of its tag, and its metadata and checksums match it.

version, and checks the image's SHA-256 against it (answer 1). That is
the app's change, not the firmware's; the owner makes it in the app.

  writing can leave no runnable app. FM-1-RE records a recovery through

## The raw image

| Rule | Value |
|------|-------|
| Format | A flat binary: the bytes of the code window, from its first byte. No header, no ELF. |
| Load address | The image's first byte is at `0x02000000`, the start of the code window. Link it there. |
| Entry | Core 0 starts at `0x02000000`: the image's first instruction. |
| Size | 1 byte to 1 032 192 bytes (1 MiB less 16 KiB). |
| The flash chip | 1 MiB. Erased (all `0xFF`) unless `--flash FILE` gives its first bytes. The image is then written into it at offset `0x4000`, as an installed image sits. Since 0.6.0 an erase or program takes time and keeps the chip busy ("The flash chip", below). |
| Past the image | Reads in the code window after the image's last byte show the flash chip: window address `0x02000000 + n` shows chip offset `0x4000 + n`. Changes the image makes to the chip (erase, program) show through the window, also over the image's own bytes. |
| Writes to the window | Ignored (and listed as unmodelled accesses). |
| RAM | 1 MiB at `0x01C00000`, all zero at the start. Other memories, and what the real chip has: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| Core 0 at the start | User mode. Every register is 0, both stack pointers included (set your own stacks first), except `r0` = `0x01C7FC00`: a 64-byte block of zeros whose first word holds `0x01C7FC40`. |
| Core 1 | Does not run until the image releases it (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md` says how). Then it runs alongside core 0 (below, "Time"). |

input.content:
### The release format (format 1.0)

Written by the spec side (session spec-overnight-1025) for the firmware
side's release tooling and the F-Emulator app to build to. "Must" is a
rule a writer or reader breaks only by changing the format's version.
Numbers in the container are little-endian; offsets and sizes are in
bytes.

**Why a container of our own, not a zip.** iOS has no public API that
reads a zip archive, so the app would need a zip reader of its own, and
Files offers to expand a file it knows as a zip archive instead of handing
it to the app. A fixed header and two byte ranges take a few lines to read
and verify, and are reproducible byte for byte without fixing timestamps
or compression settings.

#### `release.json`

One JSON object (RFC 8259), UTF-8 without a byte-order mark. Format 1.0's
fields:

| Field | Type | Required | What |
|-------|------|----------|------|
| `format` | object `{"major": int, "minor": int}` | yes | The release format's version: `{"major": 1, "minor": 0}`. Must equal the container header's. |
| `kind` | string | yes | `"app"`: a release for the F-Emulator app. (`"hardware"` is kept for M10's packages; a reader of format 1 refuses any other value.) |
| `name` | string | yes | `"small-beeps"`. |
| `version` | string | yes | The release's version, Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 without build metadata (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, optionally `-prerelease`), from 0.9.0 (answer 6). |
| `tag` | string | yes | The signed git tag the release was built from (`v0.9.0`, `m9`). |
| `git_commit` | string | yes | The tag's commit, 40 lowercase hex digits. |
| `targets` | array of strings | yes | Where it runs: `["f-emulator-app"]`. A reader that is not one of the targets refuses the release. |
| `image` | object | yes | The raw image, below. |
| `image.file` | string | yes | Its file name in the release, `small-beeps-<version>.bin`: ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_` only, no path. |
| `image.size` | integer | yes | Its size in bytes, 1 to 1 032 192 (docs/HARNESS.md, "The raw image"). |
| `image.sha256` | string | yes | Its SHA-256, 64 lowercase hex digits. |
| `image.load_address` | integer | yes | `33554432` (`0x02000000`, HW-1). |
| `image.entry` | integer | yes | `33554432` (`0x02000000`, HW-2). |
| `fwtest` | object | yes | The runner the release's tests passed on. |
| `fwtest.version` | string | yes | fwtest's version (`fwtest version`), as `0.7.0`. |
| `fwtest.image` | string | yes | The pinned image, as `config/fwtest-image` holds it at the tag (`ghcr.io/...@sha256:<64 hex>`). |
| `record` | object | yes | The test record of the tag's commit (`tools/record.py`). |
| `record.tree_sha256` | string | yes | The record's tree hash, 64 lowercase hex digits. |
| `record.ci_run` | string | no | The URL of the CI run that made the record. |
| `build` | object | no | How the image was built. |
| `build.toolchain_sha256` | string | no | The pinned toolchain's SHA-256 (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md). |
| `build.container` | string | no | The build container's image digest (R-REPRO-2). |
| `build.ram_used` | integer | no | RAM the image uses (data, bss and stacks), from the build's size report. |
| `store` | object | no | The patch store the image keeps (docs/STORE-FORMAT.md). |
| `store.format_version` | integer | no | The store format's version, so a user knows whether saved patches carry over. |
| `store.offset`, `store.size` | integer | no | Its flash region, a chip offset and a size in bytes. |

Rules:

- **No time and no host details.** No field holds a build date, a time, a
  user or machine name or a local path: the file must come out the same
  from every rebuild of the tag. The date is the tag's.
- **Exact bytes.** Written as Python's
  `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=True) + "\n"`
  does: keys sorted, two-space indent, `", "` and `": "` separators as that
  call writes them, ASCII only, one final newline. Integers in decimal
  (JSON has no hex). At most 65 536 bytes.
- **Unknown fields.** A writer of format 1.0 writes only the fields above.
  A reader ignores fields it doesn't know (a later 1.x may add optional
  ones) and refuses a release that lacks a required field or has one of
  the wrong type.
- The loose `release.json` in the release is byte for byte the one inside
  the `.fm1img`.

#### The `.fm1img` container

File name `small-beeps-<version>.fm1img`. Three parts, in this order, and
nothing after the last:

1. **The header**, 64 bytes in format 1.0:

   | Offset | Size | Field | Format 1.0 value |
   |--------|------|-------|------------------|
   | 0 | 8 | magic | the bytes `46 4D 31 49 4D 47 0D 0A` (`FM1IMG`, CR, LF) |
   | 8 | 2 | `format_major` | 1 |
   | 10 | 2 | `format_minor` | 0 |
   | 12 | 4 | `header_size` | 64 |
   | 16 | 4 | `json_offset` | 64 (= `header_size`) |
   | 20 | 4 | `json_size` | the size of `release.json` |
   | 24 | 4 | `image_offset` | `json_offset + json_size`, rounded up to a multiple of 16 |
   | 28 | 4 | `image_size` | the raw image's size |
   | 32 | 32 | `payload_sha256` | SHA-256 of every byte from `header_size` to the end of the file |

2. **`release.json`**, `json_size` bytes at `json_offset`, then zero bytes
   up to `image_offset` (0 to 15 of them).
3. **The raw image**, `image_size` bytes at `image_offset`, byte for byte
   `image.file`. The file ends at `image_offset + image_size`.

The magic's CR LF catches a file mangled by a text-mode transfer; the
16-byte alignment is for convenience only. One input gives one file:
there is no timestamp, compression or optional padding to vary.

#### The format's version

- `format_major` changes when a reader of the old version would read the
  file wrongly: the header's layout, the parts' order, a required field's
  meaning, or a new required field. A reader refuses a major it doesn't
  know ("this release needs a newer app").
- `format_minor` changes for additions an older reader may ignore: an
  optional `release.json` field, or header bytes after offset 64 (a
  larger `header_size`; `payload_sha256` still covers everything from
  `header_size` on). A reader takes any minor of a major it knows; it
  locates every part by the header's offsets and sizes, never by
  assuming 64.
- `release.json`'s `format` always equals the header's two numbers.
- This document is the format's definition; a change to it changes the
  version as above and says what changed.

#### How the app verifies it

In this order, stopping at the first failure with a message naming it,
and never running an image that failed a step:

1. The file is at least 64 bytes and starts with the magic. (Otherwise:
   not a small-beeps release.)
2. `format_major` is 1. (Otherwise: needs a newer app.)
3. The header is consistent: `header_size` >= 64; `json_offset` >=

- **No time and no host details.** No field holds a build date, a time, a
  user or machine name or a local path: the file must come out the same
  from every rebuild of the tag. The date is the tag's.
- **Exact bytes.** Written as Python's
  `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=True) + "\n"`
  does: keys sorted, two-space indent, `", "` and `": "` separators as that
  call writes them, ASCII only, one final newline. Integers in decimal
  (JSON has no hex). At most 65 536 bytes.
- **Unknown fields.** A writer of format 1.0 writes only the fields above.
  A reader ignores fields it doesn't know (a later 1.x may add optional
  ones) and refuses a release that lacks a required field or has one of
  the wrong type.
- The loose `release.json` in the release is byte for byte the one inside
  the `.fm1img`.

#### The `.fm1img` container

File name `small-beeps-<version>.fm1img`. Three parts, in this order, and
nothing after the last:

1. **The header**, 64 bytes in format 1.0:

   | Offset | Size | Field | Format 1.0 value |
   |--------|------|-------|------------------|
   | 0 | 8 | magic | the bytes `46 4D 31 49 4D 47 0D 0A` (`FM1IMG`, CR, LF) |
   | 8 | 2 | `format_major` | 1 |
   | 10 | 2 | `format_minor` | 0 |
   | 12 | 4 | `header_size` | 64 |
   | 16 | 4 | `json_offset` | 64 (= `header_size`) |
   | 20 | 4 | `json_size` | the size of `release.json` |
   | 24 | 4 | `image_offset` | `json_offset + json_size`, rounded up to a multiple of 16 |
   | 28 | 4 | `image_size` | the raw image's size |
   | 32 | 32 | `payload_sha256` | SHA-256 of every byte from `header_size` to the end of the file |

2. **`release.json`**, `json_size` bytes at `json_offset`, then zero bytes
   up to `image_offset` (0 to 15 of them).
3. **The raw image**, `image_size` bytes at `image_offset`, byte for byte
   `image.file`. The file ends at `image_offset + image_size`.

The magic's CR LF catches a file mangled by a text-mode transfer; the
16-byte alignment is for convenience only. One input gives one file:
there is no timestamp, compression or optional padding to vary.

#### The format's version

- `format_major` changes when a reader of the old version would read the
  file wrongly: the header's layout, the parts' order, a required field's
  meaning, or a new required field. A reader refuses a major it doesn't
  know ("this release needs a newer app").
- `format_minor` changes for additions an older reader may ignore: an
  optional `release.json` field, or header bytes after offset 64 (a
  larger `header_size`; `payload_sha256` still covers everything from
  `header_size` on). A reader takes any minor of a major it knows; it
  locates every part by the header's offsets and sizes, never by
  assuming 64.
- `release.json`'s `format` always equals the header's two numbers.
- This document is the format's definition; a change to it changes the
  version as above and says what changed.

#### How the app verifies it

In this order, stopping at the first failure with a message naming it,
and never running an image that failed a step:

1. The file is at least 64 bytes and starts with the magic. (Otherwise:
   not a small-beeps release.)
2. `format_major` is 1. (Otherwise: needs a newer app.)
3. The header is consistent: `header_size` >= 64; `json_offset` >=
   `header_size`; `json_size` is 2 to 65 536; `image_offset` >=
   `json_offset + json_size`; `image_size` is 1 to 1 032 192;
   `image_offset + image_size` is exactly the file's size; every sum
   computed without overflow.
4. The SHA-256 of bytes `header_size` to the end equals `payload_sha256`
   (the file was not damaged in transfer).
5. `release.json` parses as one JSON object in UTF-8 with every required
   field of the right type; its `format` equals the header's; `kind` is
   `"app"`; `targets` holds `"f-emulator-app"`.
6. `image.size` equals `image_size`, and the SHA-256 of the image's bytes
   equals `image.sha256`.
7. `image.load_address` and `image.entry` are both `33554432`.

Then the app shows `name`, `version` and the first 12 digits of
`git_commit`, and boots the image as it boots a raw `.bin` today. A bare
`.bin` still opens as before, with no version shown.

What the checks prove: that the file is whole and the image is the one
its metadata names. They don't prove who made it: the hashes travel in
the same file. Authenticity comes from the signed tag and the
reproducible build: anyone can rebuild the tag and compare `image.sha256`
and the `.fm1img`'s own SHA-256 with `SHA256SUMS` (R-REPRO-4). Signing the
container itself is left for a later major version if it is ever needed.

#### Opening it in one tap (iOS)

What the app declares, so that a `.fm1img` from Files, AirDrop, Mail or a
Safari download opens in it directly:

- An **exported type** (`UTExportedTypeDeclarations`) with an identifier
  under the app's own bundle identifier (the owner's choice, say
  `<bundle id>.fm1img`), filename extension `fm1img`, conforming to
  `public.data` only. Not `public.zip-archive` or `public.archive`: it
  isn't one, and Files would offer to expand it.
- A **document type** (`CFBundleDocumentTypes`) for that identifier with
  `LSHandlerRank` `Owner`, so the app is the default for it.
- `LSSupportsOpeningDocumentsInPlace` false, so the app gets its own copy
  (AirDrop and Mail deliver one anyway), and handles it where it handles
  an opened URL, running the checks above.
- On GitHub the file is served as `application/octet-stream`; the
  extension, not the type, makes iOS hand it to the app.

#### What the release tooling checks

The firmware side's release tool (and its tests) must show: building the
same tag twice gives byte-identical `.fm1img`, `.bin` and `release.json`;
the container passes every check above; its `release.json` and image are
byte for byte the loose files; `SHA256SUMS` matches every file. A small
reference reader in `tools/` that runs the checks above in the same order
lets the tests and the app's author agree on them.

import hashlib, json, struct, sys
MAGIC=b"FM1IMG\r\n"
def write(img, meta):
    meta=dict(meta); meta["image"]=dict(meta["image"], size=len(img), sha256=hashlib.sha256(img).hexdigest())
    js=(json.dumps(meta, indent=2, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=True)+"\n").encode()
    io=(64+len(js)+15)//16*16
    payload=js+b"\0"*(io-64-len(js))+img
    h=MAGIC+struct.pack("<HHIIIII",1,0,64,64,len(js),io,len(img))+hashlib.sha256(payload).digest()
    assert len(h)==64
    return h+payload
def read(b):
    if len(b)<64 or b[:8]!=MAGIC: return "not a release"
    ma,mi,hs,jo,js,io,isz=struct.unpack_from("<HHIIIII",b,8)
    if ma!=1: return "newer app"
    if not(hs>=64 and jo>=hs and 2<=js<=65536 and io>=jo+js and 1<=isz<=1032192 and io+isz==len(b)): return "header"
    if hashlib.sha256(b[hs:]).digest()!=b[32:64]: return "damaged"
    m=json.loads(b[jo:jo+js].decode("utf-8"))
    if m["format"]!={"major":ma,"minor":mi} or m["kind"]!="app" or "f-emulator-app" not in m["targets"]: return "meta"
    im=b[io:io+isz]
    if m["image"]["size"]!=isz or hashlib.sha256(im).hexdigest()!=m["image"]["sha256"]: return "image"
    if m["image"]["load_address"]!=0x02000000 or m["image"]["entry"]!=0x02000000: return "addr"
    return "ok "+m["version"]
img=open(sys.argv[1],"rb").read()
meta={"format":{"major":1,"minor":0},"kind":"app","name":"small-beeps","version":"0.9.0","tag":"v0.9.0","git_commit":"0"*40,
 "targets":["f-emulator-app"],"image":{"file":"small-beeps-0.9.0.bin","load_address":33554432,"entry":33554432},
 "fwtest":{"version":"0.6.0","image":"ghcr.io/x/y@sha256:"+"0"*64},"record":{"tree_sha256":"0"*64}}
a=write(img,meta); b=write(img,meta)
print(a==b, len(a), read(a))
bad=bytearray(a); bad[-1]^=1; print(read(bytes(bad)))
EOF
python3 -I $S/fmt/ref.py $S/fwbuild/app.bin

What:    Vendor patch 0012: the USB core's access port (JL_USB->CON1,
         0x11804) reads back the last access with bit 15 (MACK, done)
         set; a read (bit 14, MC_RNW) gives the byte last written to its
         index, the interrupt flags (2-6) 0. New test image usbport.c,
         the crate and harness tests usb_port_answers, suite case
         usbport; fwtest 0.7.0. HW-86 (the port, from the SDK and RE),
         HARNESS.md "USB" and Versions, EMULATOR-PARITY.md's row and
         check, harness/upstream/fm1-emu-usb-port.md, UPSTREAM.md (with
         the missing 0010 and 0011 lines), PROVENANCE P-59.
Why:     The F-Emulator app found the port never answers (its note, P-59),
         so firmware waits out its own timeout on every access; fwtest
         and the app keep the same model (docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md).
How:     Behaviour confirmed first: SDK usb.h (CON1 bits 14 and 15),
         WL82.h (JL_USB at 0x11800), usb_phy.h (the MUSB indexes); RE
         06-usb.md section 2.1 (the same indexed access in the stock
         firmware). The patch is written here from the note's behaviour;
         the flag values and the kept bytes are modelling choices, so
         labelled. The driver's own code is in the SDK's prebuilt
         libraries and was not opened.

         harness suite PASS on a local build; usb_port_answers fails
         without the patch (crate: bit 15 never set; harness: every poll
         ran out, 1000). The patches applied to the pinned upstream give
         the vendored files (fetch-emulator.sh --fetch). The firmware
         suite at cf07f9e5 on fwtest 0.6.0 (pinned) and 0.7.0 (local
         image): PASS on both, all 2202 output files identical,

content.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""Spec-side text discipline (R-SEP-1, check C-SEP-TERMS).

  check-emulator-terms.py [--show]

Looks for identifiers that occur in vendor/emulator/ and nowhere in
vendor/jieli-sdk/ or (since M4b) vendor/plaits/, in the places the firmware
side reads:
  - every tracked text file outside vendor/emulator/, harness/, sessions/
    (transcripts), docs/prompts/ (prompts are kept verbatim) and
    vendor/plaits/ (third-party code we didn't write, since M4b; its
    SOURCE.md, which we write, is scanned since SR-4);
  - the two doors, docs/HARNESS.md and docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md, and their
    reviews in docs/reviews/, for identifier-shaped words only: they carry
    addresses and other numbers on purpose, each one sourced, and people
    review them too (R-SPEC-2);
  - the commit messages in COMMIT_RANGE (default ..HEAD);
  - the pull request's title and body, when GITHUB_EVENT_PATH names one.

The list is built at run time from vendor/emulator/ and never written down:
identifier-shaped words (with an underscore, inner capitals, or letters and
digits mixed; four characters or more, not just hex digits) and hex numbers
of four digits or more, except universal constants (powers of two, 2^n-1,
2^n+1, sign-bit masks and IEEE 754's standard patterns: universal(), by
rule, since SR-4's note). Terms that already occur in CLEAN_BASELINE's tree
(the repository as the clean side left it at the end of M0a, before any
emulator source entered it) or in vendor/jieli-sdk/ (whole identifiers, or the parts of one between
underscores) are not on the list. Since M4b (the owner's decision) neither
are the terms of vendor/plaits/, Mutable Instruments' Plaits, MIT, built
the same way as the SDK's, but only from the files vendor/plaits/SHA256SUMS
lists, each matching its hash (the pinned upstream tree, R-REPRO-7); if any
doesn't, the check fails. The output says how many emulator-only terms the
Plaits list takes off (a count, never the terms). A hit is reported as its place and a SHA-256 prefix of the word, never
the word or the text around it, because the log is visible to the firmware
side; `--show` prints the word too, for a spec-side author fixing it.

A hit is accepted without an entry of its own when the term occurs in one of
the two doors as they are on main (DOOR_FILES at origin/main, or at the
commit DOORS_REF names): what is there passed people's review. The doors are
read from that commit's blobs, never from the working tree, so a branch
cannot get a term accepted by adding it to a door; a term new to a door is
still a hit until the change that adds it has merged. When that commit
can't be found, nothing is accepted this way (and the output says so).
Any other reviewed false positive is listed by its hash in
config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json, with a reason that doesn't name it.

Where vendor/emulator/ isn't on disk (a clean folder), it says SKIP.
"""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))

git add -A && git commit -q --amend -F - <<'EOF'
harness: fwtest 0.7.0, the USB core's register access port answers

What:    Vendor patch 0012: the USB core's register access port
         (JL_USB->CON1) reads back the last access with bit 15 (MACK,
         done) set; a read (bit 14) gives the byte last written to its
         index, the interrupt flags (indexes 2-6) 0. A new test image
         (usbport.c), a crate test and a harness test, a suite case;
         fwtest 0.7.0. HW-86 (the port, from the SDK and RE), HARNESS.md
         "USB" and Versions, EMULATOR-PARITY.md's row and check,
         harness/upstream/fm1-emu-usb-port.md, UPSTREAM.md (with the
         missing 0010 and 0011 lines), PROVENANCE P-59.
Why:     The F-Emulator app found the port never answers (its note, P-59),
         so firmware waits out its own timeout on every access; fwtest
         and the app keep the same model (docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md).
How:     Behaviour confirmed first from the SDK's USB headers (CON1's bits
         14 and 15, JL_USB's base, the MUSB indexes) and RE 06-usb.md
         section 2.1 (the same indexed access in the stock firmware). The
         patch is written here from the note's behaviour; the flag values
         and the kept bytes are modelling choices, so labelled. The SDK's
         driver code is in its prebuilt libraries and was not opened.
Result:  emulator crates 45 + 7 + 25 tests pass, harness 17 + 27 pass,
         harness suite PASS on a local build; the new crate and harness
         tests fail without the patch (crate: bit 15 never set; harness:
         every poll ran out, 1000). The patches applied to the pinned
         upstream give the vendored files (fetch-emulator.sh --fetch).
         The firmware suite at cf07f9e5 on fwtest 0.6.0 (pinned) and
         0.7.0 (local image): PASS on both, all 2202 output files
         identical, result.json differing only in the version. The image
         publishes on merge; the pin PR follows. check-emulator-terms
         PASS.

### The release format (format 1.0)

Written by the spec side (session spec-overnight-1025) for the firmware
side's release tooling and the F-Emulator app to build to. "Must" is a
rule a writer or reader breaks only by changing the format's version.
Numbers in the container are little-endian; offsets and sizes are in
bytes.

**Why a container of our own, not a zip.** iOS has no public API that
reads a zip archive, so the app would need a zip reader of its own, and
Files offers to expand a file it knows as a zip archive instead of handing
it to the app. A fixed header and two byte ranges take a few lines to read
and verify, and are reproducible byte for byte without fixing timestamps
or compression settings.

#### `release.json`

One JSON object (RFC 8259), UTF-8 without a byte-order mark. Format 1.0's
fields:

| Field | Type | Required | What |
|-------|------|----------|------|
| `format` | object `{"major": int, "minor": int}` | yes | The release format's version: `{"major": 1, "minor": 0}`. Must equal the container header's. |
| `kind` | string | yes | `"app"`: a release for the F-Emulator app. (`"hardware"` is kept for M10's packages; a reader of format 1 refuses any other value.) |
| `name` | string | yes | `"small-beeps"`. |
| `version` | string | yes | The release's version, Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 without build metadata (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, optionally `-prerelease`), from 0.9.0 (answer 6). |
| `tag` | string | yes | The signed git tag the release was built from (`v0.9.0`, `m9`). |
| `git_commit` | string | yes | The tag's commit, 40 lowercase hex digits. |
| `targets` | array of strings | yes | Where it runs: `["f-emulator-app"]`. A reader that is not one of the targets refuses the release. |
| `image` | object | yes | The raw image, below. |
| `image.file` | string | yes | Its file name in the release, `small-beeps-<version>.bin`: ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_` only, no path. |
| `image.size` | integer | yes | Its size in bytes, 1 to 1 032 192 (docs/HARNESS.md, "The raw image"). |
| `image.sha256` | string | yes | Its SHA-256, 64 lowercase hex digits. |
| `image.load_address` | integer | yes | `33554432` (`0x02000000`, HW-1). |
| `image.entry` | integer | yes | `33554432` (`0x02000000`, HW-2). |
| `fwtest` | object | yes | The runner the release's tests passed on. |
| `fwtest.version` | string | yes | fwtest's version (`fwtest version`), as `0.7.0`. |
| `fwtest.image` | string | yes | The pinned image, as `config/fwtest-image` holds it at the tag (`ghcr.io/...@sha256:<64 hex>`). |
| `record` | object | yes | The test record of the tag's commit (`tools/record.py`). |
| `record.tree_sha256` | string | yes | The record's tree hash, 64 lowercase hex digits. |
| `record.ci_run` | string | no | The URL of the CI run that made the record. |
| `build` | object | no | How the image was built. |
| `build.toolchain_sha256` | string | no | The pinned toolchain's SHA-256 (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md). |
| `build.container` | string | no | The build container's image digest (R-REPRO-2). |
| `build.ram_used` | integer | no | RAM the image uses (data, bss and stacks), from the build's size report. |
| `store` | object | no | The patch store the image keeps (docs/STORE-FORMAT.md). |
| `store.format_version` | integer | no | The store format's version, so a user knows whether saved patches carry over. |
| `store.offset`, `store.size` | integer | no | Its flash region, a chip offset and a size in bytes. |

Rules:

- **No time and no host details.** No field holds a build date, a time, a
  user or machine name or a local path: the file must come out the same
  from every rebuild of the tag. The date is the tag's.
- **Exact bytes.** Written as Python's
  `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=True) + "\n"`
  does: keys sorted, two-space indent, `", "` and `": "` separators as that
  call writes them, ASCII only, one final newline. Integers in decimal
  (JSON has no hex). At most 65 536 bytes.
- **Unknown fields.** A writer of format 1.0 writes only the fields above.
  A reader ignores fields it doesn't know (a later 1.x may add optional
  ones) and refuses a release that lacks a required field or has one of
  the wrong type.
- The loose `release.json` in the release is byte for byte the one inside
  the `.fm1img`.

#### The `.fm1img` container

File name `small-beeps-<version>.fm1img`. Three parts, in this order, and
nothing after the last:

1. **The header**, 64 bytes in format 1.0:

   | Offset | Size | Field | Format 1.0 value |
   |--------|------|-------|------------------|
   | 0 | 8 | magic | the bytes `46 4D 31 49 4D 47 0D 0A` (`FM1IMG`, CR, LF) |
   | 8 | 2 | `format_major` | 1 |
   | 10 | 2 | `format_minor` | 0 |
   | 12 | 4 | `header_size` | 64 |
   | 16 | 4 | `json_offset` | 64 (= `header_size`) |
   | 20 | 4 | `json_size` | the size of `release.json` |
   | 24 | 4 | `image_offset` | `json_offset + json_size`, rounded up to a multiple of 16 |
   | 28 | 4 | `image_size` | the raw image's size |
   | 32 | 32 | `payload_sha256` | SHA-256 of every byte from `header_size` to the end of the file |

2. **`release.json`**, `json_size` bytes at `json_offset`, then zero bytes
   up to `image_offset` (0 to 15 of them).
3. **The raw image**, `image_size` bytes at `image_offset`, byte for byte
   `image.file`. The file ends at `image_offset + image_size`.

The magic's CR LF catches a file mangled by a text-mode transfer; the
16-byte alignment is for convenience only. One input gives one file:
there is no timestamp, compression or optional padding to vary.

#### The format's version

- `format_major` changes when a reader of the old version would read the
  file wrongly: the header's layout, the parts' order, a required field's
  meaning, or a new required field. A reader refuses a major it doesn't
  know ("this release needs a newer app").
- `format_minor` changes for additions an older reader may ignore: an
  optional `release.json` field, or header bytes after offset 64 (a
  larger `header_size`; `payload_sha256` still covers everything from
  `header_size` on). A reader takes any minor of a major it knows; it
  locates every part by the header's offsets and sizes, never by
  assuming 64.
- `release.json`'s `format` always equals the header's two numbers.
- This document is the format's definition; a change to it changes the
  version as above and says what changed.

#### How the app verifies it

In this order, stopping at the first failure with a message naming it,
and never running an image that failed a step:

1. The file is at least 64 bytes and starts with the magic. (Otherwise:
   not a small-beeps release.)
2. `format_major` is 1. (Otherwise: needs a newer app.)
3. The header is consistent: `header_size` >= 64; `json_offset` >=
   `header_size`; `json_size` is 2 to 65 536; `image_offset` >=
   `json_offset + json_size`; `image_size` is 1 to 1 032 192;
   `image_offset + image_size` is exactly the file's size; every sum
   computed without overflow.
4. The SHA-256 of bytes `header_size` to the end equals `payload_sha256`
   (the file was not damaged in transfer).
5. `release.json` parses as one JSON object in UTF-8 with every required
   field of the right type; its `format` equals the header's; `kind` is
   `"app"`; `targets` holds `"f-emulator-app"`.
6. `image.size` equals `image_size`, and the SHA-256 of the image's bytes
   equals `image.sha256`.
7. `image.load_address` and `image.entry` are both `33554432`.

Then the app shows `name`, `version` and the first 12 digits of
`git_commit`, and boots the image as it boots a raw `.bin` today. A bare
`.bin` still opens as before, with no version shown.

What the checks prove: that the file is whole and the image is the one
its metadata names. They don't prove who made it: the hashes travel in
the same file. Authenticity comes from the signed tag and the
reproducible build: anyone can rebuild the tag and compare `image.sha256`
and the `.fm1img`'s own SHA-256 with `SHA256SUMS` (R-REPRO-4). Signing the
container itself is left for a later major version if it is ever needed.

#### Opening it in one tap (iOS)

What the app declares, so that a `.fm1img` from Files, AirDrop, Mail or a
Safari download opens in it directly:

- An **exported type** (`UTExportedTypeDeclarations`) with an identifier
  under the app's own bundle identifier (the owner's choice, say
  `<bundle id>.fm1img`), filename extension `fm1img`, conforming to
  `public.data` only. Not `public.zip-archive` or `public.archive`: it
  isn't one, and Files would offer to expand it.
- A **document type** (`CFBundleDocumentTypes`) for that identifier with
  `LSHandlerRank` `Owner`, so the app is the default for it.
- `LSSupportsOpeningDocumentsInPlace` false, so the app gets its own copy
  (AirDrop and Mail deliver one anyway), and handles it where it handles
  an opened URL, running the checks above.
- On GitHub the file is served as `application/octet-stream`; the
  extension, not the type, makes iOS hand it to the app.

#### What the release tooling checks

The firmware side's release tool (and its tests) must show: building the
same tag twice gives byte-identical `.fm1img`, `.bin` and `release.json`;
the container passes every check above; its `release.json` and image are
byte for byte the loose files; `SHA256SUMS` matches every file. A small
reference reader in `tools/` that runs the checks above in the same order
lets the tests and the app's author agree on them.

# Upstream note: the USB core's access port never answers

For the owner to offer to `joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` if wanted. Spec side
only; not filed by a session. The F-Emulator app found it and already
carries a fix (its branch `stock-016`, `f60b86b`, test `usb_port_answers`
in fm1-soc), described in a behaviour-only note the owner dropped
(PROVENANCE P-59). Written in session spec-overnight-1025 (2026-10-26)
against commit `43ed5580064885e93bc8d20be931ae950d10cd4f`; our copy carries
the same behaviour, written here from that note, as
`vendor/emulator/patches/0012-usb-port-answers.patch` (fwtest 0.7.0).
docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md lists it.

## What the chip does

A firmware reaches the USB core's (MUSB-style) registers through one
word, `JL_USB->CON1` at 0x11804:

- **write a register:** write `index << 8 | byte`, bit 14 clear;
- **read a register:** write `index << 8`, bit 14 (`MC_RNW`) set;
- then poll the word until bit 15 (`MACK`) is set; a read's byte is then
  in bits 0-7.

Sources: the JieLi AC79 SDK at `5fa84a9b`:
`include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/WL82.h` lines 15-16, 464-485 (`JL_USB`
at `lsfr_base + map_adr(0x18, 0)` = 0x11800, `CON1` its second word);
`include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/usb.h` lines 42-44 (`USB_CON1`: `MC_RNW`
14, `MACK` 15) and 148-150 (`musb_read_usb`, `musb_write_usb`);
`include_lib/driver/device/usb/usb_phy.h` lines 61-90 (the indexes: 0
`FADDR`, 1 `POWER`, 2-5 `INTRTX1/2`, `INTRRX1/2`, 6 `INTRUSB`, 7-11 their
enables, ...). The functions themselves are in the SDK's prebuilt
libraries, not in its source, and were not opened. AL-255/FM-1-RE's
`docs/io/06-usb.md` section 2.1 describes the same port in the FM-1's
stock firmware: `(idx<<8)|val`, "sign-bit completion" (bit 15 of the
halfword), with the same index map. The AC63 SDK's `usb.h` for five other
JieLi chips also has `MACK` at 15 (corroboration only).

## What upstream does

The word is plain storage: it reads back what was written, so bit 15
never sets unless the firmware wrote it. Every access waits out the
firmware's own poll limit; the app's note counts about 19 000 polls each,
and a USB stack that then retries about once a second.

## What the patch does

- Reading 0x11804 gives the last value written with bit 15 set.
- For a read (bit 14 set), bits 0-7 hold the register's byte: 0 for the
  interrupt flags (indexes 2-6), since nothing is on the bus and nothing
  is pending; for any other index the last byte written to it (0 before
  any write). These two are modelling choices, not facts from the
  sources: on the chip the flags clear when read and the other registers
  have their own reset values and read-only bits.
- A write (bit 14 clear) keeps bits 0-7 as that index's byte. The index
  is bits 8-13 (0-63).
- Nothing else changes: no interrupt, no bus events (reset, connect,
  suspend, SOF), no endpoint FIFOs, and the rest of the USB block reads
  as before. A firmware waiting for a bus event waits forever, as with no
  cable.

Crate test `usb_port_answers` (the app's test's three checks, plus an
index never written and a halfword read); fwtest's harness test of the
same name and suite case `usbport` (image `tests/images/usbport.c`: each
access polled at most 1000 times; without the patch every poll runs out).

## Left open

FM-1-RE names bit 2 of the word before it (0x11800, `CON0`) the port's
"busy" bit; the SDK names that bit `USB_NRST` (the core's reset). Neither
the app nor fwtest models a busy bit.
